quick.summary: How building for extreme situations makes your product better for absolutely everyone.
quick.takeaway: Solve for the hardest context. The benefits will always spill over.

parts.title: Design for the edges

beats.line: Why spend a whole week on high contrast if barely anyone needs it?
Think about the sloped ramps on city sidewalks.
They were originally built just for people in wheelchairs.
But delivery workers with heavy carts use them all the time.
Parents pushing strollers love them too.
We call this the universal design principle.
Can I just say helping one helps everyone?
That works perfectly. Build for the edge, benefit the center.
Okay. But how does high text contrast help a person with perfect vision?

parts.cliff: Find out why a sunny day is your biggest enemy.

beats.line: Imagine looking at your phone outside on a really bright summer day.
The sun creates terrible glare on the glass.
Right. Suddenly your perfect vision is severely limited by the environment.
High contrast makes the text readable through the glare.
So a disability is not always a permanent health condition.
Exactly. Sometimes it is just the place you are in right now.
Like trying to watch a video in a loud room.
That is when everyone turns on the captions.
So I am designing for contexts, not just permanent conditions.
And that makes your product stronger for every single user.

quiz.question: Which scenario is an example of a situational impairment?
options: Having a broken arm in a cast.
Holding a squirming baby in one arm.
Experiencing hearing loss due to age.
quiz.explanation: Holding a baby temporarily limits your mobility, changing how you interact with a product in that moment.

quiz.question: Designing for edge cases only benefits a small minority of your users.
quiz.explanation: Features designed for specific needs, like captions or high contrast, are frequently used by everyone in tricky environments.
